slides.title: The Same Story, Different Film
slides.transcript: Module 1 · Lesson 2. Documentary form and creative choice. What Makes a Good Documentary?

slides.title: Today’s destination
slides.transcript: By the end of this lesson, you can recognize six documentary approaches without treating them as rigid boxes; read a short documentary as a set of deliberate choices; retell one story in more than one form; and choose a provisional form for your own short—and name an alternative.

slides.title: Begin with story
slides.transcript: A documentary is never only its subject. The same subject can become radically different films.

slides.title: Topic + story + form
slides.transcript: Topic: the broad area. Story: what unfolds for whom. Form: how we will encounter it. Form is not decoration added after filming. It shapes what you seek, record, and withhold.

slides.title: Form is a relationship
slides.transcript: Form is the creative agreement between filmmaker, contributor, and viewer. Who speaks? Who looks? Who knows? Who is changed by the encounter?

slides.title: Use forms as lenses
slides.transcript: Documentary forms overlap. Most films are hybrids. Name the dominant logic—then notice what else the film borrows.

slides.title: Watch choices—not just content
slides.transcript: What can we see happening now? Who carries the story—and who controls its telling? Where do tension, surprise, or change enter? What do camera, edit, archive, narration, and sound make us feel or believe? What access and ethical choices made these moments possible?

slides.title: Observational
slides.transcript: Stay close to unfolding behavior and let action carry meaning. Look for sustained scenes and real-time action; limited overt explanation; and meaning built through selection and juxtaposition. What can happen without being arranged?

slides.title: Issue-led / expository
slides.transcript: Organize evidence and argument so the audience can follow a claim. Look for a governing question or argument; interviews, records, archive, or narration; and evidence arranged for clarity and consequence. What must the audience understand—and why now?

slides.title: Participatory
slides.transcript: Let the encounter between filmmaker and contributor become part of the film. Look for questions, exchanges, or collaboration; the filmmaker’s presence affecting events; and knowledge emerging through relationship. What does the encounter reveal?

slides.title: Reflexive
slides.transcript: Make the process, construction, or uncertainty of documentary visible. Look for the making of the film entering the film; evidence and representation being questioned; and gaps, limits, or contradictions remaining visible. How is this account being made—and where does it fail?

slides.title: Poetic
slides.transcript: Build meaning through rhythm, association, image, and sound. Look for mood, texture, pattern, and metaphor; nonlinear or associative structure; and sound and image carrying ideas beyond explanation. What can be felt before it is explained?

slides.title: Performative / personal
slides.transcript: Use lived experience and embodied point of view as a way of knowing. Look for first-person or situated perspective; memory, identity, emotion, or embodiment; and the maker’s experience shaping the inquiry. Why is this story being told from here, by this person?

slides.title: The useful label
slides.transcript: Hybrid is not an escape hatch. It is a pattern of deliberate borrowing. What is the film’s dominant logic—and what does each borrowed form add?

slides.title: The community garden may close
slides.transcript: One story: The community garden may close. People · place · labor · records · uncertainty · time. Now change the form.

slides.title: Observational version
slides.transcript: Spend the final open weekend with the gardeners as they work, wait, disagree, and prepare to leave. Camera: present for sustained action; little explanation in the moment. Story pressure: the approaching closure reorganizes ordinary behavior.

slides.title: Issue-led version
slides.transcript: Use the garden’s possible closure to investigate who controls neighborhood land—and who benefits. Camera: gather interviews, public records, meetings, maps, and observable consequences. Story pressure: competing claims about value, ownership, and public good.

slides.title: Participatory version
slides.transcript: The filmmaker joins the effort to save the garden and records how participation changes access and understanding. Camera: questions, collaboration, and the filmmaker’s decisions remain audible or visible. Story pressure: can the filmmaker participate without disguising influence or making false promises?

slides.title: Reflexive version
slides.transcript: Build the film around contradictory accounts—and the missing documents needed to know why the garden may close. Camera: show searches, refusals, gaps, edits, and the limits of what can be verified. Story pressure: the attempt to tell the story becomes evidence about power and knowledge.

slides.title: Poetic version
slides.transcript: Compose a sensory elegy from soil, hands, voices, seasons, empty beds, and the sounds of surrounding construction. Camera: collect image and sound motifs; build rhythm, association, and contrast. Story pressure: loss is felt through what changes in the place and its soundscape.

slides.title: Performative / personal version
slides.transcript: A gardener tells the history of the place through the plants, objects, and memories that shaped her own life. Camera: first-person narration, embodied action, family archive, and intimate encounter. Story pressure: the possible closure challenges identity, memory, and belonging.

slides.title: What stays—and what changes?
slides.transcript: Stays: the garden and closure threat; core people and place; access and ethical obligations. Changes: what counts as evidence; filmmaker presence; camera and sound behavior; structure, authority, and feeling.

slides.title: Short documentaries to study
slides.transcript: Ten Meter Tower: observe behavior, hesitation, repetition, and change. The Housekeeper: study character, labor, routine, and social context. Street Lessons: track point of view, place, and lived experience. The Queen of Basketball: notice archive, interview, revelation, and emotional structure.

slides.title: More approaches to explore
slides.transcript: Three Thousand: consider archive, sound, time, memory, and poetic form. My Dead Dad’s Porno Tapes: analyze personal narration, objects, animation, and family archive. Perfecting the Art of Longing: examine intimacy, waiting, image design, and uncertainty.

slides.title: Move from response to evidence
slides.transcript: What stayed with you—and which exact moment created that response? What is the film’s story, not merely its topic? What form dominates? What other approaches does it borrow? How are scenes, interviews, archive, narration, image, and sound used? What is one strength, one limitation, and one lesson for your own film?

slides.title: Build three films from one story
slides.transcript: Explore the supplied community-garden story world. Choose three forms. For each, define filmmaker presence, evidence, scene strategy, image, sound, and ethical pressure. Compare two versions side by side. Export a non-scored reflection summary. The test is not ‘Which version is best?’ It is ‘What film does each set of choices make possible?’

slides.title: Choose provisionally—not permanently
slides.transcript: Primary form: Which form best serves the story you can actually access and film? Alternative form: What would another form reveal—or protect—that your first choice might miss? Name the access test or small experiment that will help you decide.

slides.title: Where is the film now?
slides.transcript: Which form best serves the story? What could a second form contribute? What access or scene uncertainty must you test next? Form is a decision about how to meet reality.
